name: Cyber Hygiene for Customer-Facing Bank Employees

questions.prompt: A customer at your counter asks for a printed form located at a shared printer across the branch. What should you do before stepping away from your workstation?
questions.explanation: Locking your terminal prevents anyone nearby from viewing customer data or making unauthorized entries while you are away.
options: Lower the monitor brightness completely so passersby cannot easily read the display
Minimize the customer profile window so only the desktop background remains visible
Lock your workstation before stepping away from the counter
Ask the teller at the neighboring window to glance over at your screen occasionally

questions.prompt: You receive an email claiming to be from IT Helpdesk at support@examplebank-help.com urging you to verify your teller credentials before your shift ends. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Reporting suspicious messages through approved tools without clicking links helps security teams block threats across the bank.
options: Report the email via the bank phishing tool without clicking the link
Reply to ask the sender for their internal employee number and supervisor name
Open the link inside a private browser window just to check the page layout
Forward the message to every teller at your branch so they stay alert

questions.prompt: Which clean-desk practices protect customer data while serving walk-in clients at the counter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Keeping screens angled away, turning paper records face down, and disposing of printouts securely reduce accidental visual and physical exposure.
options: Turn printed account statements face down when not actively reviewing them
Keep yesterday's signed deposit slips in an open counter tray for fast reference
Angle your monitor away from the customer queue and public waiting area
Place unwanted customer printouts in a locked shredding bin per bank policy
Ask customers to state their full card PIN aloud when the lobby seems quiet

questions.prompt: Match each social engineering tactic a caller or visitor might use with its primary goal.
questions.explanation: Recognizing common manipulation tactics helps staff pause and follow standard verification controls rather than rushing.
left: Creating artificial urgency about a locked account
Claiming to be a senior executive calling from an airport
Leaving an unlabeled USB drive in the branch break room
Complimenting a teller's helpfulness before asking for an exception
right: Intimidating staff into bypassing standard verification
Building rapport to lower skepticism toward a risky request
Pressuring the employee to act before checking procedures
Getting an employee to plug an untrusted device into a work PC

questions.prompt: Place these steps in the correct order when a branch employee accidentally clicks a suspicious link in an email.
questions.explanation: Stopping further interaction, isolating the device per bank policy, notifying IT quickly, and documenting details limit potential damage.
options: Disconnect the workstation from the network or follow containment steps per bank policy
Document the sender address, time clicked, and any actions taken
Stop interacting with the webpage immediately and avoid entering any credentials
Notify the IT security or service desk promptly through an approved channel

questions.prompt: Compare the two internal email notices below. Select all red flags that appear in Evidence B but not in Evidence A.
questions.explanation: Lookalike sender domains, urgent deadlines, and links requesting credentials are strong indicators of phishing.

a.Subject: Scheduled System Maintenance Tonight
a.Body: Core teller systems will update from 23:00 to 01:00. No action is required from branch staff. View details on the staff intranet.

b.Subject: URGENT: Mandatory Password Sync Required
b.Body: Your teller access expires in 2 hours. Click http://login-examplebank.net/sync and enter your employee ID and current password.

options: The notice mentions branch staff and teller systems
The sender uses a lookalike external domain rather than examplebank.com
The message references scheduled overnight maintenance hours
The email applies urgent time pressure and asks for credentials via a link
The subject line includes the word Maintenance

questions.prompt: A courier in an unbranded jacket arrives at the counter holding a parcel and asks you to buzz him through the staff door so he can drop it off in the back office. Select all SAFE actions.
questions.explanation: Keeping restricted doors closed and following official visitor verification and escort procedures protect staff areas from unauthorized entry.
options: Keep the secure staff door closed and verify the delivery through official channels
Let him into the staff corridor as long as you watch him walk toward the back
Hold the door open briefly while he checks his clipboard near the teller drawers
Follow visitor sign-in and delivery reception procedures per bank policy
Escalate to a branch supervisor if the courier pressures you for unverified access

questions.prompt: Branching scenario - Urgent Caller Request. Work through three decisions.
questions.explanation: Never bypass identity verification under pressure or urgency, and always document and escalate suspicious calls per bank policy.

nodes.prompt: A caller claiming to be Mr Sharma says an ATM abroad retained his card and asks you to read his balance and update his mobile number immediately without verification because his flight boards in 15 minutes. What do you do?

options.text: Update the mobile number quickly so he can receive one-time codes before boarding
Explain politely that full identity verification is required per bank policy before discussing or changing account details
Read out his current balance as a courtesy while refusing to change the phone number

nodes.prompt: The caller raises his voice and threatens to complain to your branch manager unless you waive the verification check just this once. What do you do?

options.text: Maintain verification requirements and offer to transfer him to a supervisor or official verification channel
Ask him to state only his home city so you can grant a one-time exception

nodes.prompt: Mid-call, you realize you already disclosed account information or altered a detail without completing standard verification. What do you do?

options.text: Quietly undo the change or ignore it because the caller sounded convincing
Flag the account immediately and report the unverified action to your supervisor and fraud team per bank policy

nodes.prompt: When you offer to connect the caller to a supervisor, he abruptly hangs up. What do you do?

options.text: Move directly to the next customer without making notes since nothing was disclosed
Log the suspicious call attempt on the customer profile and alert your supervisor per bank policy
Call the number back from your personal mobile phone to check if he still needs assistance

nodes.prompt: Your supervisor asks how the unauthorized disclosure or change occurred during the call. What do you do?

options.text: Explain accurately what happened so the security team can protect the account promptly
Say the system must have glitched during the conversation

questions.prompt: A colleague forgot their smartcard at home and asks to borrow yours for two minutes to process an urgent customer withdrawal. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Sharing authentication credentials or tokens undermines individual accountability and creates serious fraud and audit risks.
options: Log in with your card and stand right beside them until they finish
Share your PIN only for this transaction and reset it immediately afterward
Allow them to use your active session while you assist another customer nearby
Decline and direct them to request temporary access per bank policy

questions.prompt: A walk-in customer hands you a personal USB flash drive containing scanned proof-of-address documents and asks you to print them from your counter PC. How should you respond?
questions.explanation: Untrusted external media can introduce malware onto bank networks; approved digital submission channels keep systems protected.
options: Insert the drive briefly, copy only the PDF files, and run an antivirus scan later
Decline to connect the external drive and offer approved submission channels
Plug the drive into a backup workstation that sits away from the main counter
Ask the customer to open the drive themselves so you can verify the filenames first

questions.prompt: You notice a customer trying to peek over the counter partition while you enter an authorization code on a shared branch tablet. Which habits help protect sensitive inputs and displays? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Shielding entries, maintaining privacy filters, and signing out after each task minimize shoulder-surfing and session hijacking risks.
options: Increase browser zoom substantially so nearby visitors can inspect account labels
Shield the keypad or screen with your body or hand while entering PINs or codes
Confirm privacy filters remain fitted properly on customer-facing workstations
Save branch portal passwords in the tablet browser to speed up busy queues
Log out of shared branch devices immediately after finishing the task

questions.prompt: Order the steps for securely ending your shift on a shared teller workstation.
questions.explanation: Closing customer records, signing out completely, securing physical items, and confirming the lock screen protect accounts between shifts.
options: Secure any physical tokens, keys, and paper records per bank policy
Close open customer profiles and active banking applications
Verify the screen displays the lock or login prompt before leaving the counter
Sign out of your user session rather than leaving it minimized

questions.prompt: Match each customer-facing banking situation with the most appropriate privacy safeguard.
questions.explanation: Tailoring safeguards to each physical or digital scenario helps keep customer information confidential across the branch.
left: Discussing a declined loan application with a customer at an open desk
Disposing of misprinted account statements containing customer addresses
Sending a customer's scanned tax form to an internal underwriting team
Leaving a branch desk for a lunch break while awaiting a customer's return
right: Use approved internal encrypted channels rather than personal email
Store files in a locked drawer and lock the computer screen
Place documents in a locked cross-cut shred bin per bank policy
Move the conversation to a private booth or lowered-voice area

questions.prompt: Compare the two login prompts shown on a branch browser. Select the ONE statement that explains why Evidence B is suspicious.
questions.explanation: Legitimate bank portals require encrypted HTTPS connections and belong strictly to official bank domains.
options: Evidence B includes the word login at the end of the web address
Evidence B loads inside a browser window instead of a desktop shortcut
Evidence B uses unencrypted HTTP and an external domain
Evidence B omits the word teller from the visible browser path

questions.prompt: You receive an email with an attachment named Updated_Fee_Schedule.xlsm from an external sender claiming to be a regulator, urging you to enable macros to read new rates before opening the branch. Select all SAFE actions.
questions.explanation: Macro-enabled attachments from unverified senders are a common malware delivery method; avoid opening them and verify updates internally.
options: Open the spreadsheet and click Enable Content so you are ready for customer questions
Keep the attachment unopened and avoid enabling macros on the file
Report the suspicious email to the bank security team per bank policy
Transfer the file to a personal device to inspect it outside the bank network
Reply to the sender requesting that they resend the schedule as a plain PDF
Check official internal notices to confirm whether any fee update was issued

questions.prompt: Someone calls the branch claiming to be from the bank's IT vendor and asks you to read out the asset tag and IP address of your counter PC to push an urgent patch. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Attackers often gather internal system details through pretext calls; vendor requests must go through verified internal IT channels.
options: Decline to share system details and direct the caller to the IT service desk
Share only the asset tag number since it appears on the outer computer casing
Ask for their company name and provide the details if the name sounds familiar
Restart the counter PC while on the phone so they can check its online status

questions.prompt: A regular customer at the counter asks you to check whether their adult child's account holds enough funds to cover a check they are about to deposit. What is the right response?
questions.explanation: Bank privacy rules prohibit sharing account details or balances with third parties—even family members—without verified authorization.
options: Confirm only whether the funds are sufficient without stating the exact dollar balance
Reveal the child's balance briefly if both customers share the same residential address
Decline to disclose any information about another person's account without authorization
Ask the customer to write a signed consent note on the back of the deposit slip

questions.prompt: Which actions help prevent tailgating and unauthorized physical access in a bank branch? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Ensuring doors latch, wearing badges appropriately, and challenging unbadged visitors in staff zones maintain strong physical access control.
options: Ensure staff-only doors latch completely behind you when entering or exiting
Wear your employee badge visibly inside staff zones and remove it off premises
Prop open the rear delivery door briefly while unloading boxes of deposit slips
Politely challenge unfamiliar visitors without a badge in restricted areas per bank policy
Hold the staff door open for anyone carrying bank-branded folders out of courtesy

questions.prompt: You assist a customer with digital banking enrollment on a branch lobby tablet, then step away to greet a new arrival without clearing the browser. What is the primary risk?
questions.explanation: Unclosed sessions on shared lobby devices can allow the next user to view or modify the previous customer's private information.
options: The tablet battery will deplete rapidly if a browser tab stays active overnight
The next customer could view or alter the previous customer's personal data
The branch wireless network speed will drop noticeably for nearby teller terminals
The tablet may permanently disable all employee login accounts automatically

questions.prompt: Compare the two customer callback verification records below. Select all red flags in Evidence B that indicate a potential social engineering attempt.
questions.explanation: Insisting on an unverified phone number while applying pressure and refusing standard checks are classic callback fraud warning signs.

a.Verification: Verified via registered callback number on file

b.Verification: Caller insisted on using a new temporary number provided during the call
b.Notes: Threatened complaint if delayed; refused branch visit

options: The caller insisted on using an unverified phone number provided during the call
The request involves confirming a wire transfer for a customer
The customer's surname is recorded in the verification log
The caller used urgency and complaint threats to pressure staff to skip standard checks
The caller refused standard verification alternatives such as an in-branch check

questions.prompt: Put the steps in the correct order when handling a phone call from someone claiming to be an internal auditor requesting remote access to your workstation.
questions.explanation: Refusing remote access on inbound calls, verifying identity independently via internal directories, and reporting the attempt stop pretext compromises.
options: Inform the caller you will verify their identity through internal bank channels before taking action
Report the unverified contact attempt to your manager and IT security per bank policy
Decline to install remote tools or share screen control on the incoming call
Contact IT or Audit via an independently looked-up internal directory number to confirm legitimacy

questions.prompt: Branching scenario - Vendor Invoice Attachment. Work through three decisions.
questions.explanation: Verify unexpected billing notices through approved procurement channels, never open untrusted ZIP attachments, and report incidents immediately.

nodes.prompt: In the branch mailbox, you see an email from OfficePrint Services saying your statement paper order is frozen over an unpaid invoice, with a ZIP attachment and a payment link. What do you do?

options.text: Download and extract the ZIP file to compare the branch order number
Click the payment link just to see which vendor portal loads
Leave the attachment and link unopened, and verify the order through the bank's approved procurement channel

nodes.prompt: Procurement confirms no order is on hold and notes the sender domain differs slightly from the real vendor. What do you do?

options.text: Delete the email quietly so nobody else at the branch opens it
Report the email with the bank's phishing tool and alert nearby colleagues per bank policy

nodes.prompt: After extracting the ZIP file and clicking the file inside, a command window flashes briefly on screen and vanishes. What do you do?

options.text: Check your open windows quickly and continue serving the next waiting customer
Stop using the PC, avoid further logins, and alert IT security and your supervisor immediately per bank policy

nodes.prompt: The security team asks whether anyone else at the branch clicked or replied to the email. What do you do?

options.text: Check with your branch manager and team and record the report details as requested
Forward the original attachment to all tellers so they know what to avoid

nodes.prompt: IT isolates your workstation and asks exactly which file you opened and when. What do you do?

options.text: Say the terminal froze on its own so nobody blames you for opening the ZIP file
Share the exact email details, filename, and timestamp so IT can contain any malware fast
Restart the workstation twice first to see whether the symptom clears

questions.prompt: Why is prompt reporting of an accidental security or privacy mistake—such as emailing a statement to the wrong customer—vital in banking?
questions.explanation: Early reporting allows security and privacy teams to contain exposure, notify affected parties, and reduce potential financial harm.
options: It guarantees the employee receives exemption from annual refresher training
It eliminates the need for IT security teams to review access logs
It automatically deletes emails already delivered to external providers
It enables rapid containment to limit customer harm and data exposure

questions.prompt: Match each workstation habit with the specific cyber risk it helps prevent.
questions.explanation: Everyday habits like locking screens, using privacy filters, and restricting add-ons address distinct physical and digital threats.
left: Locking the screen every time you leave the counter
Using a privacy filter on a customer-facing monitor
Installing only IT-approved browser extensions
Shutting down or signing out fully at end of shift
right: Unauthorized data scraping or malicious browser add-ons
Walk-up tampering or unauthorized transactions on an open session
Overnight access by cleaning staff or unauthorized visitors
Shoulder surfing by customers waiting in the queue

questions.prompt: You accidentally hand a printed account summary belonging to Ms Chen to the next customer in line, Mr Silva, who notices the error at the door and returns the paper. Select all SAFE actions.
questions.explanation: Securing returned records, reporting the privacy incident per bank policy, and recording accurate facts ensure proper customer protection.
options: Thank Mr Silva, secure the printout immediately, and verify all pages were returned
Shred the paper quietly and avoid reporting since the document was returned
Report the misdirected customer document as a privacy incident per bank policy
Ask Mr Silva to sign a sticky note promising he did not read any balances
Document accurate details so compliance can assess if customer notification is required

questions.prompt: When setting a new passphrase for a work account where system policy permits, which approach gives the strongest protection?
questions.explanation: Long, unique passphrases composed of unrelated words resist guessing and credential-stuffing attacks far better than short variations.
options: Appending the current calendar year to the end of your previous password
Combining your branch code with your birth month and middle initials
Creating a long unique passphrase from unrelated words used nowhere else
Reusing your personal online banking password so you remember it easily at work

questions.prompt: A branch uses bank-managed mobile phones and tablets for customer onboarding. Which practices follow good cyber hygiene? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Keeping managed devices updated, locking them away overnight, and reporting losses promptly protect customer and corporate data.
options: Keep the device operating system and approved apps updated per IT schedules
Connect the tablet to a nearby cafe public Wi-Fi if the branch connection slows
Store shared mobile devices in a locked cabinet overnight rather than on the counter
Report a missing or stolen branch tablet immediately per bank policy
Install a personal chat app on the tablet to send customers quick reminders

questions.prompt: Compare the two email drafts prepared by a relationship officer before clicking Send. Select all data-handling issues present in Evidence B that are avoided in Evidence A.
questions.explanation: Standard email is unsafe for sensitive account numbers, credit reports, or ID numbers, and exposing multiple clients in the To field breaches privacy.

a.Subject: Your Mortgage Inquiry
a.Body: Dear Ms Patel, please upload your payslips using our secure customer portal.

b.Subject: Re: Mortgage Details - Acc #449012
b.Body: Please review your attached report and reply with your national ID number.

options: The email includes a polite greeting addressed to a customer
Two unrelated customers appear together in the visible To address field
Sensitive account numbers and a credit report are sent over plain unencrypted email
The subject line refers to mortgage details
The customer is asked to send a sensitive identity number back via plain email

questions.prompt: Place these actions in the correct sequence when you discover you just sent an email with a customer's statement to the wrong external recipient.
questions.explanation: Stopping further messages, alerting management and incident teams immediately, sharing exact facts, and following remediation steps minimize exposure.
options: Notify your supervisor and the privacy or security incident team immediately per bank policy
Follow team instructions regarding customer notification and preventive controls
Provide exact details of the recipient address and attachment without altering logs
Stop sending further replies on the thread and preserve the sent email for review

questions.prompt: You receive a text message on your work phone appearing to come from the bank's HR team about a bonus update, containing a shortened link. Why are shortened URLs especially risky?
questions.explanation: URL shorteners mask the real target domain, making it easy for attackers to disguise fraudulent login pages as trusted links.
options: They automatically bypass the smartphone's biometric or PIN lock screen
They hide the true destination domain until the link is clicked
They disable cellular encryption for all outgoing voice calls on the device
They convert plain text messages into executable programs upon delivery

questions.prompt: Match each deceptive communication channel with its name and primary attack method.
questions.explanation: Understanding phishing, smishing, vishing, and quishing helps customer-facing staff spot social engineering across every channel.
left: Deceptive email impersonating a trusted sender
Fraudulent text message containing a malicious link
Voice call pretending to be IT support or fraud prevention
Tampered QR code sticker placed over a legitimate branch poster
right: Vishing: using vocal urgency or authority to extract secrets
Quishing: redirecting mobile scanners to a fake login site
Phishing: spoofing sender addresses or brand templates
Smishing: exploiting brief mobile alerts with hidden URLs

questions.prompt: During a busy afternoon rush, a coworker's terminal slows down and they ask you to plug your personal smartphone into the PC's USB port to tether your mobile hotspot. Select all SAFE actions.
questions.explanation: Connecting personal phones or untrusted networks bypasses corporate security controls; escalate slow systems to IT and manage queues safely.
options: Connect your phone to the counter PC via USB tethering to clear the queue faster
Decline to connect personal phones or external hotspots to bank workstations
Look up the customer's email address on your personal smartphone instead
Report the slow workstation performance to IT support per bank policy
Direct waiting customers to available colleagues or approved alternate stations

questions.prompt: How should you manage your branch access badge and physical security keys when stepping outside the building for lunch?
questions.explanation: Concealing badges outside work and securing keys prevent lost credentials from being copied or used to enter restricted areas.
options: Keep badges out of public view and never leave access items on your desk
Leave your badge clipped to your coat pocket so nearby businesses recognize you
Place your security token inside an unlocked desk drawer so it stays safe indoors
Write the staff-door PIN on the back of your badge in case you forget it

questions.prompt: Which situations should a customer-facing bank employee report promptly per bank policy? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Customer scam reports, unfamiliar hardware on kiosks, and lost badges or devices are critical indicators that security teams must investigate fast.
options: A customer reports receiving a suspicious call claiming to be from your branch
An unfamiliar cable or small adapter is spotted plugged into a lobby kiosk
A scheduled update notice appears inside the bank's official intranet portal
A bank-issued laptop or employee access badge goes missing
A customer forgets their online banking password and requests a standard reset

questions.prompt: Branching scenario - Unattended Kiosk Tampering. Work through three decisions.
questions.explanation: Never touch, unplug, or log into suspected tampered hardware; isolate it for security inspection and report facts honestly.

nodes.prompt: While opening the branch, you notice the lobby self-service tablet stand looks loose and an unfamiliar small black adapter sits between the kiosk cable and wall port. What do you do?

options.text: Unplug the unfamiliar adapter and throw it away so customers can use the kiosk
Leave the kiosk untouched, keep customers away, and alert your branch manager and security team immediately
Log into the kiosk with your employee ID to test whether the banking app still works

nodes.prompt: Your branch manager asks you to help manage the lobby while waiting for IT security to arrive. What do you do?

options.text: Place an out-of-order sign on the kiosk, leave hardware untouched for inspection, and monitor the lobby
Ask a coworker to pull out the adapter so you can photograph the pins on a personal phone

nodes.prompt: After unplugging or testing the hardware, the kiosk screen freezes and displays a connection warning. What do you do?

options.text: Stop touching the device, keep customers away, and notify your manager and IT security immediately
Plug the adapter back in quietly so IT assumes nothing was disturbed

nodes.prompt: IT security arrives and asks for your initial observations from branch opening. What do you do?

options.text: Say the cleaning crew probably bumped a cord so no further review is needed
Share exact details of what you saw, the time noticed, and relevant CCTV windows

nodes.prompt: IT security arrives and notices the cable was already moved or tested. What do you do?

options.text: Explain honestly that you unplugged or tested it before realizing the risk so they have accurate facts
Claim the kiosk was already disconnected when the previous shift closed

questions.prompt: A customer shows you a printed message claiming to be from Bank Fraud Dept instructing them to withdraw cash and hand it to a bank courier for safekeeping. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: Banks never ask customers to withdraw cash for courier pickup; recognizing this scam script helps staff protect vulnerable customers.
options: A routine high-value account audit procedure for senior account holders
A legitimate emergency cash-protection service used during core upgrades
A standard tax compliance check required before closing savings accounts
An active impersonation scam targeting the customer for cash theft

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the correct sequence when an employee discovers an unlabeled USB flash drive lying near the customer entrance.
questions.explanation: Keeping unknown USB drives unplugged, securing them away from users, handing them to security, and documenting discovery details prevent malware infections.
options: Hand the device over to IT security or branch management per bank policy
Document where and when it was found without attempting to inspect its files
Leave the USB drive unplugged from any bank computer or personal device
Pick it up carefully or isolate it so another employee or customer does not plug it in

questions.prompt: Compare the two software and extension inventories from Counter PC #4. Select all unauthorized or risky items in Evidence B that do not appear in Evidence A.
questions.explanation: Unapproved screen-recording software and third-party browser extensions can capture sensitive customer data or inject malicious code.

b.Installed Apps: TellerCore v4.2, PDF Viewer Enterprise, FreeScreenRecorder

options: An unapproved screen-recording application is installed on the workstation
TellerCore v4.2 is present on the branch workstation
Browser auto-login is configured as disabled
A third-party coupon browser extension has been added
PDF Viewer Enterprise appears under installed applications

questions.prompt: Which actions weaken multi-factor authentication (MFA) protection for bank employees? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Approving unsolicited MFA prompts, leaving hardware tokens unattended, and sharing one-time codes allow attackers to bypass second-factor checks.
options: Checking the application name and location before approving an MFA prompt
Approving an unexpected MFA prompt repeatedly just to stop the alerts
Leaving a hardware security token plugged into a shared terminal overnight
Reporting unsolicited MFA notifications to IT security immediately
Sharing a one-time code over the phone with someone claiming to be IT

questions.prompt: Match each security observation at a bank branch with the most appropriate immediate reporting or escalation path.
questions.explanation: Routing each incident type to the right specialist team ensures rapid action on cyber, physical, access, or fraud threats.
left: A suspicious phishing email arrives in the branch shared mailbox
A stranger attempts to photograph teller workstation screens from the lobby
An employee loses their bank-issued smartcard on the commute to work
A customer reports unauthorized transfers right after clicking a fake bank link
right: Escalate immediately to Fraud Operations and follow account lockdown steps
Report via the bank phishing reporting button or security mailbox
Notify IT access management and branch supervisor right away to revoke the card
Alert branch management and physical security per bank policy

questions.prompt: A well-dressed visitor arrives claiming to be a third-party printer technician for emergency maintenance on counter printers, has no work order, and asks you to sign him in without calling facilities. Select all SAFE actions.
questions.explanation: Keeping unverified visitors out of staff zones, confirming appointments via official contacts, and following escort rules prevent physical breaches.
options: Keep the visitor in the public lobby and deny access to staff zones
Let him inspect the counter printer beside you while your screen is minimized
Verify the visit directly through your branch manager or approved facilities contact
Accept a printed business card he hands you as sufficient authorization
Lend him a spare visitor badge briefly while he checks printer serial numbers
Follow vendor check-in and escort procedures per bank policy once verified

questions.prompt: A customer at the counter asks you to email their updated bank statement directly to an external accountant whose address they read out aloud. What is the safest approach?
questions.explanation: Sending statements to third parties requires proper consent verification and approved encrypted delivery channels per bank policy.
options: Email the PDF right away to the accountant's address for fast customer service
Use your personal webmail if the bank mail gateway blocks external PDF files
Follow bank policy on third-party consent and use approved secure delivery channels
Photograph the statement on your monitor and message it to the customer's phone

questions.prompt: Which risks occur when bank employees use personal cloud storage or personal webmail on branch workstations? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Personal cloud and webmail services risk leaking confidential data, bypassing bank monitoring, and introducing unvetted files into corporate systems.
options: Customer data could be leaked outside bank-controlled environments
Corporate security teams receive automatic approval to archive personal emails
Malicious files from personal accounts could bypass workflow protections
Data transfers may evade official bank audit and retention policies
Workstation smartcard readers stop functioning during customer transactions

questions.prompt: A targeted email arrives addressed to you by name and referencing your exact branch location and a local community event. What clues can still reveal a phishing attempt? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Attackers often include public details for credibility; sender domain mismatches, unusual urgency, and suspicious link destinations still expose the trap.
options: A subtle mismatch in the sender email domain or reply-to address
The email was delivered during standard branch operating hours
An unusual request to bypass normal verification or act urgently
A hyperlink whose hover preview points to an unfamiliar external site
The email uses standard business formatting without obvious spelling mistakes

questions.prompt: Arrange the actions in the right order when a customer at your counter realizes they just shared an OTP with a scammer on the phone.
questions.explanation: Responding calmly, verifying identity, triggering fraud safeguards promptly, and documenting clear follow-up details help protect the customer's funds.
options: Document incident details and remind the customer of official bank communication habits
Listen calmly without blaming the customer and verify their identity per bank policy
Initiate immediate account, card, or digital access safeguards through the fraud desk
Confirm follow-up steps and reference numbers with the customer before they leave

questions.prompt: Compare the two Wi-Fi connection screens on a bank-issued relationship manager laptop. Select all security risks present in Evidence B compared to Evidence A.
questions.explanation: Open guest networks with lookalike names, disabled VPN protection, and unrestricted auto-connect expose corporate traffic to interception.
options: The laptop screen displays the name of the active wireless network
The laptop is connected to an unencrypted open network with a lookalike guest name
Auto-connect is configured only for the corporate network
The corporate VPN is disconnected and auto-connect is enabled for all networks
The corporate network uses WPA3-Enterprise security

questions.prompt: Match each authentication mistake with its primary security consequence.
questions.explanation: Weak credential habits expose accounts to physical snooping, external breaches, unauthorized sessions, and broken audit trails.
left: Writing a workstation PIN on a sticky note under the keyboard
Reusing your corporate password on an external shopping site
Leaving a smartcard inserted in the reader while away at lunch
Sharing a login session with a trainee instead of using separate accounts
right: A breach at an external site can compromise your bank login
Audit trails cannot distinguish who performed specific transactions
Anyone near the desk can easily discover and use your credentials
Someone nearby can access your unlocked or semi-active session

questions.prompt: At closing time, you find a folder of signed customer loan applications left near the public waiting area instead of locked away. No customers remain in the lobby. Select all SAFE actions.
questions.explanation: Securing unattended records immediately and logging a privacy near-miss per bank policy allow management to review controls and protect data.
options: Secure the folder immediately inside a locked cabinet per bank policy
Place the folder on the officer's desk quietly since the lobby is already empty
Report the unattended sensitive documents as a privacy incident per bank policy
Take a photo on your personal phone to show colleagues in a chat group tomorrow
Check the surrounding area and note timeframe details if requested by your supervisor

questions.prompt: Branching scenario - Unusual Account Inquiry. Work through three decisions.
questions.explanation: Never share account data or print statements for third parties without verified authorization, and report accidental disclosures accurately.

nodes.prompt: A polite visitor at your counter asks you to print six months of statements for an elderly relative's account, saying the relative is waiting in a parked car outside. What do you do?

options.text: Explain kindly that you cannot disclose or print another person's account records without valid authorization or direct verification per bank policy
Print the statement since the visitor knows the relative's full name and date of birth
Read out only the closing balance so the visitor knows whether bills are covered

nodes.prompt: The visitor insists it is urgent and asks you to walk outside to the parked car carrying the printed statement or a branch tablet. What do you do?

options.text: Step outside alone carrying printed account records to resolve the inquiry quickly
Consult your branch manager on approved accessibility or power-of-attorney verification steps before acting

nodes.prompt: You disclosed account details or printed records without proper authorization and the visitor leaves quickly. What do you do?

questions.prompt: A local news crew enters the branch lobby holding a microphone near the entrance to interview customers about a regional outage while filming toward the teller counters. Select all SAFE actions.
questions.explanation: Enforcing branch media rules, shielding displays and records, and offering customers private booths protect confidentiality during filming.
options: Alert branch management immediately and enforce branch media/photography rules per policy
Shield active counter monitors, lock unattended screens, and keep customer papers out of view
Give an impromptu interview at the counter while customer profiles remain open behind you
Confirm to the reporter whether specific local business owners were affected today
Guide any customer wishing privacy into a closed booth away from lobby cameras

questions.prompt: Branching scenario - Suspicious Software Pop-up on Teller PC. Work through three decisions.
questions.explanation: Never run unsolicited repair or installer prompts on banking workstations; isolate the PC, escalate immediately, and report honestly.

nodes.prompt: While preparing an international wire form, your teller PC freezes briefly and pops up an unfamiliar tab prompting you to run a Security Certificate Repair Tool (.msi). What do you do?

options.text: Download and run the .msi file quickly so the wire does not miss cut-off
Stop using the PC without clicking Download or Run, and move to an approved alternate workflow
Close the pop-up tab and continue on the same terminal without telling anyone

nodes.prompt: You shift the client to a clean alternate desk while keeping the affected terminal untouched. What do you do next?

options.text: Leave the affected PC locked or isolated per policy and report the pop-up immediately to IT security and your supervisor
Plug in a colleague's personal USB antivirus scanner to clean the PC first

nodes.prompt: After running the file or staying on the suspicious PC, you see an unknown remote mouse cursor moving across the screen by itself. What do you do?

options.text: Reboot the terminal twice and see whether the cursor stops moving
Disconnect the PC from the network immediately per bank policy and call IT security and your manager right away

nodes.prompt: IT security quarantines the workstation and asks how the unexpected pop-up appeared. What do you do?

options.text: Share the exact time, what site or email was open beforehand, and confirm whether any credentials were entered
Say it looked like a routine browser update so they can close the ticket fast

nodes.prompt: IT security investigates the unauthorized remote control or file execution. What do you do?

options.text: Claim the cursor started moving randomly with no prior pop-up or download
Wait until the next shift starts to reset any passwords
Explain honestly what was clicked or run and cooperate immediately with credential resets and wire checks

questions.prompt: A branch courier arrives during a busy shift to pick up a sealed pouch of archived checks for off-site storage. What must occur before handing over the pouch?
questions.explanation: Checking courier identification and completing chain-of-custody logs prevent impersonators from walking away with physical banking records.
options: Hand the pouch over quickly across the counter as long as they wear a uniform
Leave the unsealed pouch by the side exit door so the courier grabs it faster
Verify the courier's ID and sign custody logs per bank policy
Ask a waiting customer in the lobby to witness the handover verbally
